lead: A data flow diagram (DFD) is a picture of movement. It shows the data that enters a system from outside, the processes that change it, the stores that keep it, and the data that leaves. It shows no order, timing or decisions. Analysts use it to check that every input is used and every output is produced, and to explain a system to a customer who does not read code. This chapter covers the four symbols, two levels, numbering and balancing.
prereq: You need 2.1 for what a functional requirement is, and 2.5 for the scope the diagram must stay inside.

sections.h3: Four symbols carry the whole notation

blocks.text: A DFD is a graph of four things: external entities, processes, data stores and data flows. It answers one question — where does each piece of data come from, what changes it, where is it kept, and where does it go? It is a functional model: it describes what the system does with data, not how fast or in what order. Draw it early, beside the use cases, because a customer who cannot read code can still read this.

head: Shape
Name
What it means
Rail booking example
rows: A person, device or other system outside the boundary
A transformation of input data into output data
Two parallel lines or an open box
Data at rest, written and read by processes
A named packet of data moving between symbols

items: Every process has at least one input flow and at least one output flow.
Every data store is written by some process and read by some process.
Flows carry nouns: passenger details, payment status. A verb such as validate is a process, not a flow.
No arrow joins two external entities, or two stores. Data always passes through a process.

blocks.text: You draw in levels, never a full system on one page. Level 0, the context diagram, is the whole system as a single process numbered 0, surrounded by the external entities that talk to it. It contains no data stores. Its only job is to fix the boundary: what is inside the software and what is outside.
Level 1 opens process 0 into real processes numbered 1, 2, 3. Their sub-processes are numbered 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, so the number names the parent. Two levels are enough for most requirement reviews.

items: Draw the context diagram and list every flow that crosses the boundary.
List the processes inside and number them 1, 2, 3.
Draw each process box and connect it to the stores it reads or writes.
Repeat the same external entities, and redraw every boundary flow exactly as the context diagram showed it.
Count boundary flows at both levels; the two sets must match, name for name. Flows between two child processes, or between a child and a store, are new internal detail and are always allowed.

blocks.text: F_child(X) = F_parent(X) for every external entity X
blocks.where: F_parent(X) is the set of data flows between the system and external entity X in the parent diagram; F_child(X) is the same set in the child diagram. The two must be identical. Flows inside the child, whether process-to-process or process-to-store, are extra and always allowed. This identity is called balancing.

sections.h3: What the diagram cannot say, and what a CASE tool adds

blocks.text: A DFD has no decisions, no loops, no sequence and no timing. It cannot say "if the payment fails, do not issue the ticket", because that is control, not data. For control use a state or activity model (see 2.7) or the interaction diagrams of Unit 3. A DFD says what data must exist; it never says when.

Every flow and store name is defined once, with its fields, in a data dictionary, so "booking request" means the same five fields everywhere it appears. That keeps two analysts drawing the same diagram. CASE tools store the diagram in a repository and check it mechanically, flagging:

items: A process with inputs but no output, or the reverse.
A store that is never read, or never written.
A flow whose name is missing from the data dictionary.
A child diagram whose boundary flows do not match its parent.
Two different names given to the same data.

spec.aria: A data flow diagram with entities Passenger, Railway Admin and Payment Gateway, processes 1 Enquiry, 2 Booking, 3 Cancel and 4 Maintain, and stores Train Schedule and Ticket. Pairs of solid arrows join entities to processes, 12 in all; 7 dashed arrows link processes and stores.

examples.question: A rail reservation system has three external entities — Passenger, Railway Admin and Payment Gateway — four processes — Enquiry, Booking, Cancellation and Schedule Maintenance — and two data stores — Train Schedule and Ticket. Draw the context diagram and the level-1 DFD, number the processes, and show that the two levels balance. State how many data flows each diagram has.
steps: Context: one process, numbered 0, named Rail Reservation System, with the three entities outside it. No data stores. The four processes are hidden inside process 0.
Passenger: three flows in (enquiry request, booking request, cancel request) and three out (train list, Ticket, refund status) = 6 flows.
Railway Admin: schedule update in, update status out = 2 flows.
Payment Gateway: payment request and refund request in, payment status and refund status out = 4 flows. Context total = 6 + 2 + 4 = 12 flows.
Level 1 opens process 0 into 1 Enquiry, 2 Booking, 3 Cancellation and 4 Schedule Maintenance. The entities and all 12 boundary flows are redrawn unchanged.

Internal flows are new. Maintenance writes Train Schedule (1). Enquiry reads Train Schedule (1). Booking reads Train Schedule (1). Booking writes Ticket (1). Booking sends a confirmation to Cancellation (1). Cancellation reads Ticket (1) and updates Ticket (1). Internal total = 7 flows. Each read is one arrow from the store to the process, not a query-and-reply pair.
Level-1 total = 12 boundary flows + 7 internal flows = 19 flows.
Balancing check: the 12 flows touching Passenger, Railway Admin and Payment Gateway at level 1 are exactly the 12 of the context diagram. Nothing added, nothing lost, so the child is balanced.
examples.answer: The context diagram has 12 data flows, the level-1 DFD has 19 data flows (12 boundary plus 7 internal), and the 12 boundary flows match exactly, so the two levels balance.
examples.check:
entities = 3
processes = 4
stores = 2
passenger_flows = 3 + 3
admin_flows = 1 + 1
gateway_flows = 2 + 2
context = passenger_flows + admin_flows + gateway_flows
internal = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1
level1 = context + internal
for v in (entities, processes, stores, context, level1, context):
    print(v)

traps: Drawing control inside a DFD: an arrow labelled "if seat available", or a retry loop. Conditions and order belong to an activity or state diagram.
Thinking a flow between two child processes is wrong. Booking sending a confirmation to Cancellation is legal internal detail. Only boundary flows must match the parent.
Unbalancing a child: adding a flow to Payment Gateway the parent never had, or losing "refund status" on the way down.
Drawing a read as a query arrow into the store plus a reply arrow back. A read is one arrow from the store to the process.
Showing data stores in the context diagram. Level 0 has one process and the external entities only.
Joining two stores, or two external entities, with an arrow. Data moves only through a process.
Naming a flow with a verb. "Validate booking" is a process; "validated booking" is the flow that leaves it.

quiz.q: Name the four symbols of a DFD and state what each means.
quiz.a: External entity (a source or sink of data outside the system boundary), process (a transformation of input data into output data), data store (data at rest), and data flow (a named packet of data moving between the other three).

quiz.q: Why does a DFD show no decisions, loops or sequence?
quiz.a: It is a functional model: it records what data exists and how it is transformed, not when or in what order. Conditions are control, which the diagram has no symbol for. Use an activity, state or sequence diagram for control.

quiz.q: In the rail system, the context diagram shows the flow "booking request" from Passenger to the system. Which level-1 process receives it, and which flows leave that process?
quiz.a: Process 2, Booking, receives it. Booking reads the Train Schedule store, writes a record to the Ticket store, sends a payment request to Payment Gateway, sends a confirmation to Cancellation, and returns the Ticket to Passenger. The flows touching Passenger and Payment Gateway are boundary flows that must match the context diagram.

quiz.q: A context diagram has 8 boundary flows. Its level-1 child has 8 boundary flows and 6 internal flows, but the parent flow "payment status" is missing at level 1 and a new flow "offer code" from Passenger appears. Is the child balanced? Give the corrected count and say what the count does and does not prove.
quiz.a: Not balanced. One parent flow was dropped and one the parent never had was added. Restore payment status and remove offer code (or add offer code to the parent too): 8 boundary flows plus 6 internal flows. The total is still 14 flows, because one flow is swapped for another, so the number alone hides the fault. The set of boundary flows must match, not just the count.

quiz.q: Level-1 process 3 is decomposed into three sub-processes. Write their numbers, and say how many processes the level-0 diagram has.
quiz.a: The sub-processes are 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 — the parent number is the prefix. The level-0 diagram has exactly one process, numbered 0, representing the whole system.

quiz.q: Give one question this diagram answers well and one it cannot answer at all.
quiz.a: It answers "which data stores does Booking write?" — the arrow to the Ticket store. It cannot answer "what happens if the payment fails?" — that is a decision, shown in a state or activity diagram.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern data platforms still draw this diagram: a Kafka or Spark pipeline is described as sources, transformations and sinks, which is a DFD with the arrows renamed. Security engineers feed DFDs into STRIDE threat modelling, because each flow and store is a place to ask what an attacker could read or change. Legacy-modernisation teams redraw old systems as level-1 and level-2 DFDs before touching code. Useful search terms: context diagram, levelled DFD, data dictionary, STRIDE threat model.
